review_text:
A little difficult at first, Hades quickly became addictive.

When I first started playing, I struggled quite a bit and it quickly put me off. But after giving it another try a few weeks later, I became completely obsessed with this game. I never imagined I'd end up playing for over 100 hours. I beat the game again, and again, and again, and I just couldn't get enough of it.

If you're a fan of roguelikes (or roguelites), you'll definitely find something to enjoy here. And even if it's a genre that usually puts you off, you might be pleasantly surprised. Why? Because unlike quite a few games in the genre, the difficulty curve drops considerably as you progress and unlock various upgrades. Finding it too easy after a while? No problem, you can increase the difficulty as much as you want.

Honestly, I considered Hades to be very accessible for a roguelike. Of course, I'm saying that based on my own experience. I've seen people complain that they couldn't finish a single run after 100 attempts; if you're at that point, just give up on roguelikes.

What else could I say, except that the art direction was absolutely fabulous? If you're into Greek mythology with a modern twist (yeah, because Greek mythology isn't actually just about gods and heroes happily beating the ♥♥♥♥ out of each other), you'll be in heaven.

The music in this game... OH, THE MUSIC! It was incredible, the kind of soundtrack you could listen to even when you weren't playing.

One of the reasons it was so hard to get tired of Hades was that the gameplay was incredibly varied: there were tons of weapons, boons with all kinds of different effects, and countless ways to approach a run. You never really felt like you'd seen and done everything.

If we compare it to Enter the Gungeon, sure, there's a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ of weapons and other items, but very quickly, everything starts to feel like something you've already seen before. That wasn't the case here, even though you technically, globally, go through the same rooms.

Another reason was the absolutely insane amount of things to discover and unlock. Whether it was completing a run, reaching the game's ending, discovering all the dialogue, building relationships with all the characters, buying decorations or bonuses, and so on.

I was honestly amazed by the amount of dialogue in this game. I'd done over 100 runs, with more than 75% of them successful (yeah, I was showing off, so what?) and even though I was starting to feel like I'd seen most of what the game had to offer, there were still things left for me to discover.

Hades was a true gem.

I mean what can be said of Stardew Valley that hasn't been said before? It's a solid revival of Harvest Moon-esque cozy farming games, with endearing characters, solid gameplay and progression (especially the skill level system), incredible art and music, and surprisingly interesting lore. Add the stubborn position of ConcernedApe to never make us pay for updates, and to always come back to the game even after saying "I'm done with it, onto the next project", and you get one of the most popular games of all time.

I do have nitpicks though. 
I'm kind of ticked by the gameplay loop because it seems it almost always leads to the player optimizing their in-game days down to a routine often centered around making money, taking the cozy part away entirely.
The romances are pretty one note once you've reached marriage, the spouses don't really do anything except the occasional helping hand, and will just hang around the farm the rest of the time, and I always end up feeling bad for them because I get this impression that I locked them into this life away from what they loved doing prior to marriage.

review_text:
MONTONOUS AND UNFUN. 

>>>

This game teaches you to run away from/past all of the enemies you face, mostly, and even if you work hard to learn their patterns and use the sluggish and unkind combat controls to defeat them, your reward is next to nothing. 

Seriously, I have barely found any gear or weapons worth using, most stuff you DO find is worse than the gear you probably already have. 

Many enemies don't drop enough runes to justify fighting them at all, and again your reward is nothing. 

Levelling feels like nothing changed. No tutorials or explanations force you to turn to youtube ect, and even then it makes little difference.

They worked so hard to make these areas and enemies and you may as well just run right through them.

The story is completely un-follow-able I have no idea what is going on, who is who. 

Most online tutorials just suggest cheesing and game breaking mechanics.

When you do grind out a big fight, often you are rewarded with nothing, pretty much. Once you beat the mariner boss you can go visit some guy in 'dragonbaren'  and there each enemy drops 1000 runes and is easy to kill and stun lock. Meanwhile, the vast majority of other enemies dont drop anything close to that despite being MUCH harder to deal with. 

The game encourages hit and run tactics if you do fight, due to large crowds of enemies who will stun lock and kill you, which is boring. 

Plenty of collecting and hunting to do, but I do not know what for, I am near to level 30 and have never needed to use the crafting menu. 

Most mechanics are pure mystery, just check online. 

Now, you must ask yourself, is this person who is writing this review just bad at games? not used to boss fighting games? is he just a bit salty? I have nearly 100%'d cuphead. Enjoyed it despite some rage. I have ground out many hard games, and I enjoy achievement hunting, I love a challenge. Elden ring is a monotonous bore I have no idea how I have come this far. 

The game doesn't run nearly as well as it should, my computer isnt great but can run other similar games smoothly. 

The open world aspect is whatever, I use the fast travel as much as possible and just rush through new areas avoiding absolutely everything til i find the next grace. 

I WENT INTO THIS GAME BLIND, thinking it would be fun. Do not do that. It is far too much labour to try and figure ♥♥♥♥ out for yourself, find little things in a big world and so on. Just take the advice of better players. 

I think the combat is dog**** and the controls are obnoxious, there should be a separate button for sprinting and rolling. I am using PC controls, its annoying and feels bad.

ONTOP OF THAT there is ♥♥♥♥ tons of outrage about the DLCS that I do not own being A) too expensive, nearly the cost of the base game, B) Some are effectively microtransactions, and C) Many people say to play through the base game before getting the DLCS because they don't add enough to change much of your playthrough, just new weapons and bosses locked behind a £40 paywall. 

I do NOT understand the hype at all, Its a genuinely bad game, I just wanted to level up and fight cool bosses, yet you are encouraged constantly to run away ect, go grind to avoid being one hit, then fight the boss and by your 20th attempt you might do OK. 

I could appreciate that if there were big upgrades, gear and combat pace improvements. EVERYTHING is sluggish. I have refused to use ranged weapons and magic, because THEN you really can cheese. 

Your reward? 2000 runes or so. Maybe a talisman. You beat a boss and leave the same power level you were before the fight. 

Also, the dropping runes on death is just an inconvenience, not difficult to deal with, just another chore you have to drag yourself through. The game is already so slow why try to take away people's hard work? its unlikely but why, like in games like terraria no one plays the drop items on death difficulty, because it takes forever to get stuff and people dont like that or enjoy the challenge. I just get on the horse, get my runes, and leave. Spend your runes before boss fights you cant leave. 

Yep.

review_text:
I honestly think the unlimited carry weight, removal of equipment durability, and transmog system are some of the worst changes in the remaster.

They may look like harmless quality-of-life features, but they seriously hurt the immersive RPG experience. They turn the game into something much more focused on instant gratification and “just have fun” gameplay.

I know all of these features can be turned off. But I don't think that's a good solution. Developers shouldn't add a bunch of systems that fundamentally change the way the game is played and then simply say, “If you don't like them, just turn them off.”

The problem is that these rules used to exist naturally as part of the game. Now, if I want the original experience, I have to impose those rules on myself.

Those are not the same experience.

Before, the game told me: “You have limited carry weight, so you have to think about what you pick up and what you keep.”

Now the game tells me: “You can carry everything if you want. You never have to repair your equipment if you don't want to. You can use whatever stats you want while looking like something completely different.”

And I have to tell myself: “Okay, I won't use those features because I want to play the game the old way.”

That's not the same thing. The first is a game system. The second is basically a self-imposed challenge.

I think modern game design is increasingly treating friction as something bad: if something slows the player down or forces them to make choices, it must be removed.

But in an RPG, those limitations are often exactly what give your actions meaning. **And it is precisely because the game gets in my way that my actions have meaning.**

If I have unlimited inventory, picking up another item means almost nothing. If my equipment never deteriorates, maintaining it means nothing. If appearance and equipment are completely disconnected, what I'm actually wearing no longer has to make sense in the world.

The problem isn't that these features exist. The problem is that they change the game's rules and then leave the original rules as something the player has to impose on themselves.

Even if it seems overwhelming or maybe too long for some people at start, give it some time and you will start to enjoy it sooner or later. 10/10 game and studio, I doubt anything will ever top it out (maybe The Witcher 4, but only time will tell).

review_text:
Full honesty here, I slept on this game for years because I thought people were overreacting and hyping it up too much. I bought it on sale after the release of Silksong because I wanted to see what people were losing their minds over and I figured that if I didn't like it, I bought it for so cheap that it it wouldn't really be that much of a detriment to me for spending $8. This game is genuinely the best game I've ever played; there's literally not a single thing I would change about it. The art and music are gorgeous, and the world design is great too. I loved every minute of this game and I have what I consider to be a pretty significant amount of hours in game, so that is praise is not so easily earned, but this game deserves it. 

I see a lot of people talk about how much they loved certain bosses and certain areas, but I want to talk about how perfect the difficulty scaling is. I typically tend to play a lot of puzzle games and stay away from more combat oriented games, so I was apprehensive at first about trying Hollow Knight in the first place. However, when I was making my way through the first area in the game, I encountered an enemy with a shockwave attack that I had not seen before. I died attempting to get past this enemy a few times, but I beat it after learning its attack pattern and I was proud of myself. I was very nervous coming up to the first boss since I had heard a lot about Hollow Knight's difficult bosses. As I fought this boss for the first time, I very quickly realized that the game had prepared me to fight this boss, because it had the shockwave attack that I learned to dodge from the previous enemy. Despite me sucking at the combat, I beat the boss on my first try, and it clicked for me. I understood in that moment why people praised this game so much. It teaches you everything you need to know to handle difficult bosses through exploration. And this continues throughout the game, I think that for every single boss in the game (except for the final bosses and dream bosses) the game prepares you for at least one of their attacks simply by exploring the area they're in. You will always find at least one enemy that has an attack similar to what the boss for that area will have. It's so simple in terms of game design, but genius, because it allows players like me with little to experience with combat games to be able to succeed. 

Now, obviously I love Hollow Knight a LOT because I was crazy enough to get all steam achievements, but my point is that the game design and difficulty scaling is so good that anyone can play it. If you're on the fence about getting it like I was, take this as your sign to buy the game, even if it is on sale. In hindsight, I feel bad that I only paid $8 to experience this masterpiece when now I would've gladly paid full price, heck even double the price because I loved it so much.

TLDR: Music, art, game design, and difficulty scaling is PERFECT, even for beginners. Play it!

I hate reviews that split a game's value into things like music, art, gameplay, story, sound design, etc.
Games aren't just a mass of separate pieces that can attach and detach from each other like Lego bricks. Judging the individual parts separately with no context is useless. 

To me, this game is an exception to that. It feels like a group project in school where only the level designer cared about getting an A+. The levels are just so far beyond everything else in the game, and sadly even the blunted and weirdly unexpressive movement lets it down too. If this game had a Super Meat Boy-like feature where you could see all your previous attempts superimposed on each other, they'd all look pretty much the same (at least until it introduces advanced mechanics in the post-story portion of the game). The art is good, and the music is irritatingly repetitive - I didn't see a need for that one melody to constantly feature in almost every song. The story is just a generic indie-depression story, which I'd consider a simple and effective story if it weren't for the difficulty sliders. A simple and unobtrusive story can be made great if woven together with the mechanics of the game (like Paper's Please), and this game came sadly close to achieving that. The player's experience of failing repeatedly and then finally proving to themselves that they can climb something they thought impossible is a perfect match for Madeline's story, except unlike Madeline, the player can just cheat their way through with the difficulty sliders. I don't think games, movies, music, or any media has to be made for everyone, and I do think this appeal to accesibility diminishes the story. It went from a story that only a game could tell, to the tumblr post of a self-absorbed moody teenager 

7/10

review_text:
It Takes Two is a beautifully created world filled with details and reactive environments. It follows the story of a married couple whose marriage is on the brink of collapse, and their daughter who is caught in the middle of their frustration. 

With some magical handwaving, the child's desperate wish to reconnect her parents together comes true, and a love book she found comes to life and transfers the parents consciousness into tiny dolls. Over the course of 12 hour or so, you will make you way through a massive child-like interpretation of your enchanted home. 

The story is center stage, with your characters frequently talking to each other and commenting on the world around them. Luckily the voice actors and writing are all good, and most people will get a few chuckles out of it. Second to that is the gameplay, which is made of up platforming and puzzles. Both elements are generous, with your characters able to double-jump and air-dash to get around, and the puzzles only taking a minute or two to figure out. The pacing is excellent, and the challenge is well tuned to allow all kinds of players to enjoy it. You are constantly moving into new areas, which in turn give you new abilities to solve new puzzles with. By the time you've got a good handle on the mechanics, the game moves on and give you a new world with new mechanics to explore.

The graphics deserve a special mention. The textures and detail of the world is first-class, with many familiar objects like cloth or wood taking on a new dimension of detail due to your tiny size. It is visually satifying the same way that a game like 'Yoshi's Wooly World' is. The sound design is no slouch either, with the music returning to themes and altering them to suit the changing biomes. Every surface you run on will sound the way it should, with no details being too small to include.

If you enjoy games like Mario or Little Big World, you really can't go wrong with this one. Doubly so given that only one person needs to buy the game, and a friend can join in for free.

The elephant scene in It Takes Two is, in my opinion, one of the most disturbing scenes in the entire game. It goes far beyond what is necessary to tell the story and turns cruelty and violence into entertainment.

What makes it even more concerning is that the game can be played by children and teenagers. Presenting violence in such a graphic and comedic way can potentially make cruelty seem normal or acceptable, especially to younger players who may not fully understand the distinction between fictional entertainment and real-world behavior.

The story could have delivered the same emotional impact without going this far. There were countless ways to portray the conflict without making such extreme violence the center of the scene.

This is not about being against video games or fictional violence in general. It is about questioning whether a scene this cruel was really necessary—and whether there was a better, more responsible way to tell the story.

Portal 2 is quite simply the pinnacle of puzzle adventure games and raises the bar over the original title into the stratosphere. Valve took thinking with Portals to the next level with the addition of gels and lasers, allowing you to bounce high, run fast and redirect lasers with Portals to advance through the depths of Aperture Science in fun and interesting ways. 

What’s truly mind blowing is the Portals and puzzles themselves are somehow not even the best part of this game. Valve went the extra mile to craft a quality cast of characters that leave an ever lasting impression on the player.  Throughout the game you will be subjected to some of the best writing and humor that has ever been produced in media, and a story that will hook you until the very end. Dare I say the Pixar of video games. 

Valve even included a very easy to use level editor, which allows you to create your own puzzles for the world to play, rate and comment on. Cuphead is technically a run 'n gun and shoot 'em up. It has great controls, amazing art/design. While the game can be a tad frustrating, it isn't unfair. It just requires a bit of precision, patience and practice. That said, it also brings me little fun to play.

I love run 'n guns, schumps are my favorite genre of video game. However, Cuphead's version of these are not my 'cup of tea'. Pun intended. The run 'n gun is more accurately an action platformer with shooting. With the shooting part mostly secondary until the boss fight. Certainly more Mega Man than Contra. Though stages are fairly short, and much of the time simply the boss fight. Nothing wrong with that, but I personally can't get over that I would rather play an actual run 'n gun like Gunstar Heroes instead. Which has everything Cuphead's run 'n gun has turned up to 11.

The shump stages just make me sad. I very much prefer bullet hells, but I don't mind a classic 80s/early 90s STG either. Cuphead is very much more the classic version of a shoot 'em up. But minor enemies don't really matter other than potentially removing threats. There's no score and no power ups from shooting them, It can actually be better to wait and parry their bullet to build up your super attack. And your guns are peashooters the entire time.

The run 'n gun or the shoot 'em up boss battles take too much time for me personally. I have been recently been playing classic Contra games, and I don't think any of the bosses in Contra or Super C were close to 30 seconds. Where as Cuphead bosses are usually over a minute. Even with multiple stages the bosses go through, I find my mind wander and lose focus. I'm a little bored trying to keep precise control of the character to actually knock them out. This boredom leads to some sloppy play on my part as well as disinterest in playing the game.

I get these are nitpicks and personal issues. However, despite how beautiful the art, clever the mechanics are and solid the controls are I find myself wanting to play other games close to what Cuphead does but much tighter. Things like Metal Slug, Gunstar Heroes or even one of the NES Mega Man games for run 'n gun. And Gradius, R-Type or Darius.

I'm glad Cuphead for a short time introduced new players to classic video game genres. Maybe with me already playing a ton of them, I already have a knowledge of just what sort I like and don't like. Certainly the hype around this game didn't help. But I hope to keep enough interest in playing it to beat it, but I don't know. I just don't find it particularly fun.

review_text:
[u][b]-Quick Review-[/b][/u]
Cuphead is a 2d “Run and Gun” where the first thing you’ll want to do is rebind your shoot button to something you can hold down at all times, so you can gun while you run. Then you will proceed to get beaten up by the various colorful bosses and enemies until you learn the attack patterns well enough to pass the level and move on to the next level. I felt like I ran into a brick wall until I slowly knocked each brick out and was able to limp through to introduce my face to the next wall.
Cuphead was developed by Studio MDHR Entertainment Inc and released in 2017. It’s absolutely insane that the developers took the time to make the game using “traditional methods” by HAND drawing then water coloring and having their own jazz recording. But that’s what takes Cuphead from being merely a good “run and gun” game and boosts it to an inspiring work of video game art.

[u][b]Review Video:[/b][/u]
If you don't like reading, or are curious about watching gameplay check out my video here:
https://youtu.be/mEznF6KfXcY

[u][b]-Detailed breakdown review-[/b][/u]
[b]Story:[/b] Our protagonists are Cuphead and Mugman. Apparently, they didn’t learn the lesson “gambling sucks”, and the more important rule regarding gambling which is “The house always wins”. Well, Cuphead and was on a hot streak, and made a deal with the literal Devil. The foolish little Cup got greedy and of course the dice were loaded so he lost the bet, and now you gotta help Cuphead and Mugman collect the “Soul contracts” from all the different zany characters so that the Devil will spare them.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3638041696

[b]Gameplay:[/b] Cuphead is hard, but the controls are simple, movement to the right or the left, duck by pressing down, aim up by pressing up, jump, shoot, charged, shot, switch weapon, aim mode and a dash button. the most technical part of cuphead is the parry which is used on “pink” attacks/enemies/particles. The User Interface is simple too in the bottom left you have your hit points and the status of your charged shot.
I would say there are 3 game modes: Brawls, Airplane Mode, and lastly Run and Gun. The brawls are the easiest to explain, normal controls, you carefully watch the boss to see what move they’re going to use and then dodge, think “Mega Man or Sonic the hedgehog boss fight” without the rest of the level.
The Airplane game mode is different, because you move around 2d space as an airplane this game mode feels more like a side scrolling shoot-em-up or a bullet hell. Your charge shot changes, you don’t have any charms or shot customizations, you do have a choice between shooting regular straight shot, or lobbing bombs which will arc down from your character. You also have a shrink move which shrinks your hitbox making you harder to hit… but also decreases how far your shots travel, so it’s a risk/reward kind of move.
Lastly the Run and Gun modes, which you do just that, run through a level to get to the end. Lots of different smaller enemies will drop in on you and respawn, so don’t get too comfortable staying in one place to wait and think. There are coins in the run and gun game mode which you can collect to buy equip able weapons and abilities from “Porkrind's Emporium”.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3638042497

[b]Conclusion:[/b] I really like Cuphead on several levels. The gameplay is a bit tougher then I’d prefer… however without that difficulty you could blow through the game in a couple hours, so I understand how you can get really hooked on getting good at Cuphead… especially if you invest the time to really learn the attack patterns and what cues to watch for.
And that’s about the worst I can say about cuphead. The music is really freaking classy. The old 1940’s cartoon style is *chef’s kiss*. If you’re good at 2d platformers, run and gun games, probably a lot of old classic retro console game skill would apply here. If you’re good at those I think you’re in for a real treat with Cuphead! I’ll just conclude this review by saying we’re lucky to be living in the timeline where we got such a great game!

Disco Elysium is one of those games that have been so deeply analyzed and promoted via constructive discussions, ranging from praise to criticism, to such an insane degree that the very act of writing a positive review for it is almost unnecessary. It is a game that has a distinct voice, cadence and lexicon that has produced some of the more literate reviews ever published on Steam. Meanwhile, its gameplay loop, as well as other aspects of its DNA, has done something for the genre in the same equivalence as what Dark Souls has done to melee combat. And yet, it is still rarely emulated and even rarer still, is it emulated well to any of the same degree.

A truly remarkable game, a one of a kind journey that is the direct result of unemployed hyper-literacy. The purest form of socialism available. Not only is it arguably one of the greatest contributions to media that its home nation has ever made, but the game and the developers have suffered greatly from their own success. In the end, they were betrayed by a single piece of paper more than the person who robbed them or even the legal gymnastics that justified the robbery. 

When the game was first pitched to me, it was as a true "cyberpunk" game in spirit and soul, albeit with a widely different aesthetic than what I would have expected. In all truth, Disco Elysium is certainly closer to the high brow Neuromancer more than people realize. Regardless, it is a game that is best exemplified by a low carb, carnivore focused diet. It is perhaps, clinically overweight but surely not obese nor does it suffer from bloating. It is a very dense package of muscle that has been formed from carrying its previous weight of expectations around for so long. At most, its genuine flaw is at times, too much of a good thing. The game equivalent of high cholesterol and not enough simple proteins or the occasional complex carb to balance it out. 

In all aspects, the game has an extremely strong aesthetic and a high fidelity in its own artistic vision, which the developers held in high integrity. This does, at times, means that the perspective and the environments are not always friendly to navigate and some things can be overdetailed to the point it is hard to discern things from one another or properly define the playable boundaries, but this is something to be expected of a game of its type and scope. 

What the game does well, it does better than any others. A dialogue-puzzle driven game that incorporates the best form of anti-ludonarrative dissonance proofing, merged with the best aspects of tabletop roleplaying with none of the lampooning, flanderized lameness of Critical Roll. A game that is also so utterly devoid of typical fantasy and more present in the strangereal, fantastika late and post Soviet imagination. 

A game that will frankly, be completely disregarded by some, largely those who have been frankly spoiled by modern, attention grabbing conventions and those who are easily anxious in their own impatience. But also, you will occasionally see the masterful dialogue and writing being interpreted as "bad" by simians who have never engaged with actual literature in their entire lives. The game, on the bright side, does gatekeep itself by requiring basic reading comprehension and a passive willingness to not mindlessly engage with every line of dialogue or savescumming to get a perfect outcome. 

I have played the game thoroughly and deeply several times over, at one time consecutively, both pre-final cut and post-final cut. On my most recent playthrough, I still found outcomes that utterly surprised me and actively immersed me in the unspecified anxious distress that is so perpetually present in the doomed Harrier Du Bois. One thing I can surely say is that the game will lose some people with its reliance on deeper political metaphysical comprehensions and the game's worldbuilding is as dense as its politics itself, which uses a distinct diction that can be truly incomprehensible to casual, non-political individuals in much the same way that theological, seminary-driven biblical language is hard to comprehend for those who lack an interest in it or the culture of its interpretation that many countries have in their curriculum or general upbringings. 

It is certainly a political game where its politics are its main draw and while there are many who will moan and complain that it is a communist game, it is one of the most engaging pieces of leftist self-critique ever published in any media. And it is entirely hilarious too. Communists that constantly blame their persistent infighting and windmill-chasing on one another being varying degrees of liberals, the mystifying, nearly occultic pseudo science in the deliberate misunderstandings of capital, the well intended but blissfully ignorant hyper-liberalism that rules the world, the unrepenting reactionaryism and fascism driven by idealogue-emulation or merely personal insecurities, the game actually is extremely willing to critique everyone from a deeply critical position of satire, but also earnest portrayal. 

Ultimately, a lot of people have internalized the views of their Harry or have retroactively applied their own to him and there will inevitably be people who feel a strong dislike when being mocked for their beliefs. But one must remember how the Harry character is written, how the narrative is constructed and how he is merely a vehicle for how actual ideal and conviction-driven characters actually act and apply their personal philosophy to the immediate reality around them. A recurring theme is delusion and how so much of reality really can be relative to one's mental state, and that no doubt, group mentalities can affect individualists just as much as collectivists. 

Regardless, I still think the game actually offers the most scathing criticism of communists ever penned by non-jingoist class enemies. It is a game that recognizes the failures of the institutions raised from revolution, the inherit affiliation with armed violence and insurgency with socialist thought, the consequences of socialist regimes and their failures, the failure to implement and build upon overly idealistic promises, as well as the rampant defeatism, doomerism and depressing dismay affiliated with "true believers", who in turn, gate keep them from others by producing a religion of ideology without realizing it.

Much like its critiques on religion, the game brings attention to the fallacies of self-appointed intellectuals on subjects that deal entirely in theory. And how this applies to almost every belief system and the metaphysics of border into the surreal and esoteric, but all under the encompassing veil of materialism, slogans and cults of personalities, culminating in the ironic, very consumerist hero worship of socialist figures. The game does have scathing and inherently true critiques of other systems as well as the big C-ism too, but it is all done in extremely high concept taste, as a certain Idiot Doom Spiral would say. 

It is a great game to figure out how *you* think and what beliefs you have internalized. A lot of people have played this game thinking themselves communists or fascists, only to find out they are just liberals. It is an extremely funny thing to see and even funnier thing to witness the seethe and cope that comes with it. 

That being said, Disco Elysium is a game that you absolutely should play, regardless of your beliefs. And while many will scoff and discount it as "preppy college kid socialist writing", they are actually removing themselves from a very human story, with very human characters.

Outside of the politics, there is a lot of love and hurt put into this game that few games will ever be able to emulate.

review_text:
Amazing game, lots of reading. For you normal people out there, you'll notice it didn't take me 30 hours to beat it. It took me 17- did all the sidequests and everything. I bought this game a long time ago when the Steam Deck first launched because everyone had high praise for how well it ran on it. I never got far that first time. You can see a lot of the glaze from other reviews here, so I'm going to put in a few of my nitpicks and gripes instead. Still an absolute banger that was worth playing, but I feel like a lot of people skipped over what I'm gonna say.

Yes, I did skip a fair bit of dialogue. There are SOME parts that really aren't essential to the story and you can get the gist of. That's all games and media though. I just couldn't be bothered with a lot of the faction exposition riddled throughout the early game. I know a lot of you lore lovers out there might hate me for saying it, but it really wasn't essential to the CORE of the story. The fat guy is a slimy mob boss GTA lester type of manager for his workers that are unionizing and on strike, the lady on the boat works for big corpo and wants to negotiate- I get it. There are long treks of reading, especially in your own character's mind that can really annoy you just a bit over time too At least one or two of the voices (not a fan of the whacky tie) got on my nerves. I think that's the point of the tie though.

Before any nitpicking, the attention to detail is one of the most amazing things about the game. I won't spoil anything hefty here. But, the story will hint at a certain article of clothing or even a tiny detail- and if you recall it and take advantage of it, it rewards you for it. There are about maybe three moments in the story where I changed an article of clothing and it changed how certain events played out. Least spoilery example: The first time I noticed was when I wore the Pinball Maker's coat because I thought it fit the MC. I ended up in a dialogue involving it and they pointed out I was wearing his coat. Small things like that really spoke to me.

This game was a bit of a rollercoaster for me. I'd get really into it and invested- then I'd lose a bit of interest when a more boring part would come up (talking to the dice lady). It took me three or four days to beat it all- but that was mostly because this game does wear you down. I recommend taking breaks and pacing yourself.

A few of the nitpicks I have:

Movement is HORRIBLE. Slowing down constantly when going through a narrow space, WASD was atrocious to use- sometimes making me move in a completely different direction when going down stairs or something. Felt like that wasn't really figured out. Ended up swapping to mouse, but even then.. If there is a mod for toggle on/off sprint- I'd use it.

Some portions of the game are intentionally drawn out so you can't pause and save. This is probably an intentional design to prevent save scumming, but I definitely wanted to try a few things out without having to load all the way back. Maybe it's the BG3 save scummer in me that just wants to succeed certain rolls.

Lack of autosaves is another thing. The fact that the game doesn't auto save after crucial moments or even when you sleep for the night is ridiculous. I recall dying at one point and having to reload a save- just to find out it was from the previous day. But it autosaves after I revisited a random area for the 4th time? SAVE FREQUENTLY. Losing a lot of progress will make you quit for the night.

Dice roll outcomes and their impact on the story. There was one portion of the game where I had to crack open an ice cream machine. I rolled a perfect roll and still failed. The game tells you that if you roll perfectly, it auto succeeds. Apparently a perfect roll wasn't enough and I needed a better tool. This does nothing for the story. You get the better tool later and honestly it does nothing for the rest of the story- it's JUST for opening that ice cream machine and it doesn't even really add any bonus stats for prying that machine open either. Why not let me succeed and get the item inside? It doesn't progress the main story- it's for a side mission only and I can't do anything with it because 1. I don't have the password and 2. I have to actually finish that side story to use it anyway. Yet, there's a near-impossible roll in the main story where I can just bypass all of the mystery of finding a basement and just "teleport" on top of a roof? No skillchecks or anything? I know it's comedy- but it's kinda insane that you can bypass that part of the MAIN STORY.

At the end of the game, they sort of tally up your performance throughout through dialogue. I took ONE SIP from a bottle to clear a quest from the start of the game. Yet, at the end, they talked as if I was binge drinking throughout the entire investigation. Yes, my character was an alcoholic BEFORE the game started. But I was SOBER throughout- minus the sip. I felt cheated and hated that there wasn't any way to defend my character at the end.

[SLIGHT SPOILER WARNING]

Speaking of endings, I won't say I'm UNSATISFIED. But, I wasn't fully convinced that the last guy was the actual murderer. It felt too easy and I didn't fully come down on the guy because I was convinced the game wasn't about to end so abruptly and that this was a red herring. It was, in fact, NOT a red herring. Imagine my surprise when I come back and the game is literally over. I fully expected a postgame and there wasn't one. Why not let me run around and have one last dialogue with people? Anything?

My rating is 8/10. Absolutely worth it, but not the perfect masterpiece people describe. Maybe would've been higher if I LOVED reading as much as these other guys here.

It’s excellent. Arguably one of the greatest RPGs ever released. The quality of the story, dialogue, and characters is outstanding; everything is meticulously crafted and dazzles with its sheer depth and complexity.

I appreciate how the developers—in a rather cynical manner—set out to portray various ideologies while exposing their flaws. I also really value the inclusion of rave subculture. There is over 60 hours of text in a single playthrough, even without exploring every possible option.

One cannot overlook the visuals and the beautiful art style, either. The game proves that you don't need massive graphical spectacle to captivate the player—even in this day and age.

The fact that the game focuses on conversation rather than combat is wonderful. It features the protagonist's complex inner psychological world, discussions with the aforementioned characters, and a multitude of choices and decisions. Not everything is spelled out explicitly, leaving room for interpretation.

It is a shame that, even after all this time, the game's ending still contains minor bugs; you have to reload the game to resolve them.

The ending is a bit disappointing, BUT the conversation with the perpetrator was very interesting and atmospheric.

P.S. Even the scandal surrounding the game (and the studio) fits perfectly with what *Disco Elysium* presented.

review_text:
I feel this game is trying to be Symphony of the night, Binding of Isaac and Dark Souls inside a 90’s platformer (Wonder boy 3/Aladdin etc) without really standing out as its own game. And this is why while I was playing I couldn’t connect with the game in any way that was meaningful.

Pros
- Controls/character are well refined and feel good to play
- Plenty of game content to engage with, with multiple paths to take each run

Cons
- Runs feel repetitive, with similar enemy types each run – especially the first level. To fix this the dev could change up the first let or let you pick the first level. 
- the combat felt a little unforgiving, with stuff flying at you from off screen and hitting you without warning so you would lose your skull bonus. 
- A lot of the weapons felt like “white” items from diablo – stuff you’ll never use. To fix this the dev could make weapons like dark souls – where they all can be equally as powerful.
- Progression felt grindy, especially with multiple deaths in between (which loses your progress). This could be fixed by making death less punishing.
- The difficulty curve can spike unexpectedly – for example in the vault area the gold monsters can one shot you ruining a 30 minute run. 
- $35 for a pixel art game is overpriced I feel.

I like roguelikes, but this one just wasn't for me. It has good movement and gameplay, but some of the mechanics are just plain annoying. Like how some enemies can just shoot through walls, or hit you from off screen. After a few hours of playing run after run, I was just bored. The game is also way too grindy. I like how you collect souls of fallen enemies to get upgrades, but you need SO many. Would have been nice to use gold in addition, since have the time, I have nothing worthy to spend it on and just end up using it to reroll weapon modifiers. Also, the lack of any damage mitigation upgrades severely hurt the experience, forcing you to either "git gud" or give up. Luckily, I noticed the Assist Mode in the options, which the devs suggest using if you're not having fun...and I sure wasn't. With that, I was able to beat the game (but like, only 3 bosses? really??). I'm uninstalling it for now. Maybe I'll come back to it at some point, but I'd have to be especially bored to want to play this one again.

On a side note, I was also displeased that the game has side areas that lead to areas only accessible if you own the DLC's. I was on a run trying to get to the exit in the time limit for bonus rewards in a new area. I was cutting it close and when I saw the elevator, I took it up, only for the game to tell me to buy the DLC for that area. When I made it to the actual exit, I was past my time window by like 10 seconds. If I don't own the DLC, just remove the elevator from that spot. Don't waste my time.

A relentless surge of momentum defines this experience, delivering fast, fluid action that feels sharp from the very first encounter. Every run unfolds through shifting pathways, dangerous foes, and cleverly arranged arenas that reward quick thinking and confident movement. The constant push forward creates an addictive rhythm where each attempt feels meaningful, energetic, and full of possibility.

Combat stands out with crisp responsiveness, impactful feedback, and a wide arsenal that encourages experimentation. Weapons, skills, and mutations stack into endlessly varied builds, transforming each run into a fresh strategic puzzle. Permanent upgrades ensure steady long term growth, turning every defeat into progress and reinforcing a satisfying loop of learning, adapting, and improving.

Environmental variety remains impressive, offering dense secrets, branching routes, and beautifully crafted zones that shift with each attempt. High tempo traversal blends seamlessly with challenging enemy patterns, creating a flow that feels both demanding and exhilarating. The overall structure balances roguelike unpredictability with metroidvania style discovery, producing a hybrid design praised for its innovation and lasting appeal.

Replay value reaches exceptional heights thanks to massive content support, diverse builds, and a difficulty curve that rewards mastery without sacrificing fairness. Each run invites experimentation, risk taking, and bold playstyles, ensuring that the experience remains fresh even after countless hours. Critics consistently highlight the tight controls, stylish presentation, and addictive progression as defining strengths.

A polished, high intensity action journey emerges. One that blends precision, creativity, and challenge into a deeply rewarding loop. A strong recommendation goes to anyone seeking fast combat, meaningful progression, and a world that continually surprises with every new run.

I went and read the negative reviews first, hoping for company. Mostly nonsense, or complaints about something else entirely, and I found myself wondering whether I really wanted to stand in that queue just because the game and I didn't get along.
So: thumbs up, from someone it didn't work for. 

Here's my case, for what it's worth.
In a metroidvania the unlock pays off because the map holds still: you remember the wall you couldn't cross, and you go back for it. Dead Cells generates its rooms, so the rune you earn opens a door you never met. The reward is real, the memory isn't, and that memory is the half of the genre I came for.
Then the grind wore me down and I put it away. The difference from the grind I've complained about elsewhere is simple: here it sits underneath a game that was already excellent before you ground anything.
Which is the whole point. At some stage the quality is loud enough that personal fit stops being the argument, and I can hand this to almost anyone without a warning label. If metroidvanias and roguelites are both your thing, Dead Cells welded them together better than anyone had managed before, and it's still what everything else in that lane gets measured against.
Movement, art, sound, all of it pulling the same direction: an action game that stays light without ever feeling cheap.
Not for me and yet obviously good.

A majestic pixelated haven for my autistic drives. 
El juego no tiene un objetivo explícito; sin embargo, si conocemos los géneros sandbox y supervivencia, a medida que uno se va enfrentando a los diferentes mobs hasta tropezar con algún boss, se intuye fácilmente que hay una progresión en la que podemos ser cada vez más fuertes. Entonces llega lo importante. Lo que ves te gusta, los controles son intuitivos, suena bien y eres de los que mientras juegan se preguntan "¿Cómo puedo ser más fuerte? ¿Cuál será el siguiente boss? ¿Cómo consigo esto o aquello?" o quieren crear algo bonito o tal vez sienten la necesidad de comportarse de forma impulsiva (peleador cuerpo a cuerpo tanqueando daño) o quieren sentir que pueden causar daño sin apenas consecuencias (rango), o poner a prueba sus reacciones e ingenio con un desafío con alta recompensa (invocador), etc.; incluso, si ves jugar a alguien y piensas en que lo puedes hacer mejor, ahí ya hay una gran probabilidad de que Terraria sea para ti.
El juego es tan flexible como seas capaz de imaginar porque te da muchas herramientas. Además, hay muchas personas que aman el juego: sus creadores y su comunidad, por eso puedes esperar un entorno fascinante para vivir nuevas experiencias y retos: el mismo lugar de siempre aún te sorprende.
Terraria es casi un hogar para mí. Es hermoso.

not saying this game didnt do amazing things or that they didnt put a lot of good work into it, but this game is not for everyone, regardless of how much you think it would be. I'm someone that's been playing dungeons and dragons for a LOOOONG time. started with 3.5, but i've also played AD&D, 4e, 5e, as well as a load of other tabletop rpg's. i've played loads of rpg video games too. some of my favorite games are rpg's of one flavor or another. that being said, i cant stand baldur's gate 3. i've tried so many times, i've tried vanilla, i've tried with mods, i've tried solo, i've tried with friends, but the game just cannot keep my interest past the beginning of the second act. i've watched videos about the story of the characters i cared about, and i've seen countless speedruns, but i just cant be bothered to play the game myself. the encounter gameplay is insanely picky about positioning, breaks or does unexpected things like letting enemies fire through floors/walls, or making you miss out on just a smidge of movement in enough places that you then cant complete the action you were moving for, etc etc. also, while rolling dice is something i'm very accustomed to, i despise rng on this level in video games. i dont feel like i'm being skilled or lacking skill, i feel like i'm being cheated.
some of the characters are actually terrible too. like, most are just annoying or barely memorable at all, with only a very small handful of characters actually having good stories. some characters have good stories, but terrible personalities that just grate me in every conversation. some character's logic is not logical at all, some story telling elements are frustratingly railroaded, and the max level of 12 really brings the game down. 
obviously, there's plenty of people that love this game, and it has great reviews, but its seriously not for everyone, and with a AAA price tag, its very difficult to recommend the game to people. with my experience with rpgs both analog or digital, you'd think this would be a great title to add to my library, but i honestly regret the purchase. also because of the nature of the game, i wasnt able to get a good feel for how i'd like the game before the refund period expired too, so now its just an expensive plaque on the back shelf of my steam library.

review_text:
The best save-scumming simulator since Pathfinder: Kingmaker.

Baldur's Gate 3 looks fantastic and has all the ingredients of a great RPG: an excellent story, incredible voice acting, cinematic scenes, interesting classes, and plenty of quests. Unfortunately, the dice-based gameplay completely kills the experience for me.

So much of what you do comes down to dice rolls that even characters who are supposed to be good at something can constantly fail at it. What's the point of making a decision or building a character around certain strengths when the game can just decide that your character is suddenly incompetent?

Pros:

- Great story, graphics, and cinematic scenes that make you want to keep playing.
Probably the best voice acting I've ever heard in a game.
- Extensive and interesting class and character building.
- Lots of well-designed and memorable quests.
- The game encourages multiple playthroughs if you want to see everything.
- The amount of choices and possible outcomes is genuinely impressive.

Cons:

-The heavy reliance on dice rolls can make your character choices feel meaningless. Even with a high chance of success, you can still fail at something that should be routine.
-The constant failed rolls can turn serious situations into a comedy show. At some point you could put circus music under almost every encounter and it would fit.
-Some characters and dialogue feel more like edgy teenagers than actual adults, which can really hurt the immersion for me.
-The constant save-scumming becomes almost mandatory if you don't want important situations decided by an unlucky roll. This reminds me a lot of Pathfinder: Kingmaker.
-Loading saves repeatedly gets especially annoying when you already know that a failed roll was the only reason something went wrong.

Overall:

I understand why so many people consider Baldur's Gate 3 one of the best RPGs ever made. The production quality, voice acting, visuals, story, and character building are absolutely top-tier.

But personally, the dice system ruins too much of it for me. I prefer RPGs where character progression actually makes you reliably good at something. If my character has the skills for a task, I want that to matter instead of constantly watching him trip over his own feet because the game rolled a 1.

For me, Dragon Age: Origins and Dragon Age II are still much closer to what I want from an RPG. Baldur's Gate 3 is incredibly well-made, but the core gameplay philosophy simply isn't for me.

review_text:
An entire genre sits in the Spire's shadow. If i'm playing another game and I'm shown a map with vertically-oriented dotted lines connecting nodes, or given the option to choose one out of exactly three items / upgrades / cards, I flinch and think of the game that dwarfs what I'm playing. 

StS works so much better than its imitators because it works on so many levels - it's fun to stupidly throw cards and die in your first run, and it's fun to theorycraft and optimise every tiny move. The StS subreddit shows how bad most of the playerbase is at this game, but they still love it. Most of its imitators just see the depth and longevity of Spire's endgame, and focus their efforts on achieving that (and still fail), but the vast majority of any game's playerbase is going to be terrible at it, and the game needs to be fun for those people. 

I can't properly talk about the endgame depth since I'm nowhere near as good as the top players, but the amount of meta changes that high-level StS gameplay has seen over the years is proof of how deep it goes. There aren't many games that have had so many paradigm shifts in the absence of balance patches, fewer still if you exclude mechanical skill-based games like Melee. If Dream Quest had the endgame depth that StS did, I'd be playing Dream Quest instead of StS

If I had to find one actual "fault" with the game, I'd say it's the theming. The world doesn't feel cohesive or centralised around anything in particular. You're climbing a tower but all of a sudden you're on the streets trading with a beggar, or fighting out of a colosseum, or watching a jousting match atop a tall bridge. The enemies and characters seem to have no connection to each other beyond some vague "lore" which to me seems like a weak substitute for actual story. It's implied the Silent and the Nemesis somehow know each other, and the Watcher and the Time Eater somehow know each other, and the Awakened One is the object of worship for the cultists, maybe the Bronze Automaton is somehow related to the Defect, and maybe the Merchant fought his way up the spire too - but what's the point of any of this? None of this "lore" amounts to anything because there's no story; nothing actually happens in the game beyond just going up a tower and killing everything in it. Again this is a very minor complaint, but the theming of this game bothers me disproportionately to how much it matters, probably because I've seen some people actually praise the "lore" and even the "story" of this game. Lore isn't a substitute for story to me, it should only exist to bolster whatever happens as a result of the player. 

9/10

I don't think I've ever been so sure I would like a game, only to be so wrong. I have played for 28 hours and beat the game with each character, but I've decided to cut my losses with this one.  Veterans will praise the game's "fine balance", but that balance ONLY EXISTS for veteran players. There is no room in the game for a casual player, and until you have played 100+ hours, you will just lose (slowly) most of the time, and even when you do win, it isn't satisfying, it just feels like you had good RNG that round.

I had fun exploring the game for the first 10 hours, but it's been a chore since. I can see where the game could become more fun after 100+ hours, but I don't want to grind 100 hours of non-fun play just to get there. I'll probably look into Slay the Spire 2 when it launches, but I won't be interested if they haven's solved the issue of accessibility for learners and casual gamers.

I did like almost everything else about the game. Nice vibe, music, art, and playstyle. There is a nice variety of cards, consumables, and relics. The game could use wayyyy more enemy types, there's only like 20 different enemies you can fight and it makes each run too repetitive when you fight the same enemies, in roughly the same order, every run. 

I definitely can understand the cult following for this game, and clearly the devs did something right with all the positive reviews this game has, but if you aren't planning to spend 100 hours learning the game, it might just be better to skip it.

You can have an ok time on the game, there are things to enjoy but there is a lot to hate, it is definitely not a masterpiece, it makes Ubisoft games feel bug free in comparison, it is possibly the most overrated game ever talked of but you can still have a good time on it

review_text:
Factorio can easily be called a perfect game - it's clear the developers poured their hearts into it. It's a game about building and automating a factory, where you gradually unlock new technologies and build increasingly complex production chains. After the release of the Space Age expansion, I don't think there's anything missing, and if you ever want more, there are always mods to turn to.

If you have a tendency toward obsessive organization and planning, you'll be in seventh heaven. The game can be fairly challenging for newcomers at first, but the developers did an amazing job with how new things are gradually unlocked through research - you're never overwhelmed right from the start, but instead move through clear milestones: your first research, advanced mining, oil processing, and so on.

The Space Age expansion then adds beautiful and highly varied planets - each one brings something new, so there's always more to do.

This is one of the very few games that truly deserves a 10/10.

From a Satisfactory perspective:
What I feel Satisfactory has and this game has not:
Exploration, story/lore by ADA, beautiful handcrafted map, (very limited) beauty building and eye candy graphics.

What this game has and Satisfactory has not:
The locals actively attack you, requiring base defence and you exterminating their nests
Crazy options using circuits (I barely used this)
Higher skill/efficiency/optimization skill ceiling

In general, Factorio is more distilled automation with a higher ceiling. Your factory will be 10x the scale and there are more nobs to turn to dail in your efficiency.
I feared I wouldn't like the constant attacks, but it actually adds a nice change of pace and another set of problems to solve.

review_text:
Divinity: Original Sin 2 is a comforting game. You can see it in my hours played. It makes you want to spend time in its world and its systems.
It's not about being addictive (though it does have this "just one more area" effect), but rather inviting. Just like in DOS1, with the first notes of it's main theme, it makes you feel at ease.
The world is colorful and quirky. Even when some dark stuff happens inside it, it still looks and feels like a fairytale. For every mutilated corpse, there is an opinionated cow eager to talk (and trade) with you. DOS2 can't keep a straight face for a minute, but I would say that it is its biggest charm.
The characters have personalities that are larger than life, but main cast surprisingly has a level of depth that keeps them from being grading. I was not expecting to enjoy the company of some of the characters as much as I did.
Though in the story deprtment, even if I think that the game is a step up from the previous title, it still is a bit flat. Where the gameplay and exploration give you freedom and width of approaches, main quests usually have minimal choice branching at the end, and more often then not the choices are equally jarring. 90% of the time the choice is either "Forgive Hitler" or "Murder".
If you don't come to this game expecting fantasy epic, you can actually find a lot of gold in unexpected places. The line that stuck with me the most comes from the optional DLC with an (arguably) annoying talking squirel.
Real focus of the game is in its systems and how they facilitate exploration and combat. The maps are packed full of content. By its sheer volume, it makes moment-to-moment gameplay rewarding.
The fights are almost never boring. Even the hardest battles are not won by brute force but by tactical understanding of the battlefield. Being outleveled never was a deciding factor. Every time the enemy decimated my party, I was able to come up with a strategy for a second or a third attempt that flipped the tables completely.
Only at the tail end of the campaign, the fights sometimes become a bit too "gimmicky". By trying to give the players a different objective than just kill all enemies, devs make combat closer to "annoying puzzle" side, where you understand the solution but have to wait for the opportunity to attempt it.
Divinity: Original Sin 2 is a great sandbox, if by sandbox you mean the whole theme park. The game is exceptionally good at what it does well, and what it does not — it is quite understandable and never trully a detracting factor. With its great explorable world, engaging combat and most of all inviting atmosphere, it is an RPG to lose yourself in for an hour or a hundred.

review_text:
I played this game with my girlfriend and a close mate, and we had an absolute blast playing it. We played on Hard mode, and even though it was a struggle at many points throughout the game, we managed to beat it after putting around 100 hours into it and completing almost every quest we could.

As someone who loved Baldur’s Gate 3, there was plenty to compare between the two games, but I also loved how different they were in their own ways. I really liked the armour and magic armour system in this game because it made combat feel very different from BG3. There were also plenty of spells and abilities that felt unique, which made experimenting with different builds really fun.

The story was also really good and interesting. I loved how each character had their own way of interacting with the world and how your choices could change how certain situations played out. I played as Fane, and I think he made the story even more interesting. Playing as Fane felt very different from playing the other characters because you have to hide your identity from people and deal with the fact that you are an undead character.

I also really enjoyed how Fane's abilities affected gameplay. Having to heal yourself with poison instead of normal healing made playing him feel completely different from the other characters. It was a small thing, but it made me think differently about how I approached combat and managing my health.

Overall, I really enjoyed Divinity: Original Sin 2. Playing it with my girlfriend and my mate made the experience even better, especially because we were able to experience the story and difficult fights together. The amount of freedom, different character interactions, combat options and choices made the game feel like an adventure that we were creating together. After spending around 100 hours with it, I can definitely say it was a game I was glad I played.

review_text: Sekiro is one of the most well executed games I've ever played. The world building, combat, atmosphere, scenery and gameplay are all beyond well executed. This is not a fromsoft title that I ever found myself going "yeah that was stupid" after I died. This game always felt fair, and like you were in control. Not only is it fromsofts magnum opus of combat, it's also by far their greatest world building and lore. The world is so dynamic in this game it genuinely feels alive. After every large world event it literally affects and changes almost every aspect of the game. Backtracking to check out a previous area always feels rewarding. The cherry on top is that this game has absolutely the greatest bosses in fromsofts tenure, and the final boss is just an absolute masterclass. Cannot recommend this game enough, as long as you enjoy the fromsoft difficulty. Do not expect a soulslike however, the only thing this game shares with the souls series is the developer and the flask/bonfire mechanics. Absolutely nothing else is like the rest of the games.

review_text:
This game was my first-ever Soulsborne game. When I went into it, I was expecting quite the challenge, but I foolishly thought that it wouldn't be much harder than Jedi: Fallen Order on Grandmaster difficulty.

Then, right after getting my arm sliced off by Genichiro, I started getting my face kicked in. But I made progress.

The game was a lot harder than I thought it would be, and yet I persevered all the way until I met Lady Butterfly, who became my first true wall. At that point, my journey through Ashina led me to what seemed like unbreakable walls.

One day, after hours of constant death at the hands of the Ashina Elite, Genichiro, Lady Butterfly, the Long-arm Centipede, the Armored Warrior, and all the hordes of enemies, I finally broke. My preexisting gaming ego died, and I rage-quit the game, feeling depressed and defeated.

And yet, I kept feeling the urge to go back, pick up my shinobi katana again, and fight.

One fateful day, that urge to return and fight became irresistible, and suddenly, I was able to break through those seemingly unbreakable walls. Although I would soon come across new, seemingly impossible foes, my newfound strength allowed me to surpass them all.

Over time, this game stopped making me feel depressed because of its difficulty. Instead, I started to feel alive while playing it. Beating those seemingly impossible foes was a rush like no other.

And yet, I continued to doubt my ability to beat this game, right up until the very end, when I faced the Sword Saint.

The memory of fighting and beating the Sword Saint for the first time is one I hold close to my heart. It was not only one of the best experiences I've ever had in gaming, but also the culmination of a journey that changed my life.

The journey I underwent while playing Sekiro for the first time led me down the path of Soulsborne, and that path helped make me the man I am today.

It made me more resilient, kind, loving, and hopeful in life. The Soulsborne games lifted me up many times when I was down, helping me not go Hollow. They taught me not to hesitate in dire moments, helped me meet many wonderful friends, and ultimately led me into the loving embrace of my now-girlfriend.
Remember, shinobi: hesitation is defeat. And whatever you do, don't you dare go Hollow!!!
